en: The Ritual Text for the Bodhisattva Precepts, excerpted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang by imperial decree.

1. The Ritual for Receiving the Precepts (Śīla-karman). First: If any bodhisattvas wish to train in the three clusters of pure precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara) of a bodhisattva—whether they be householders or renunciants—and have first generated the great aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they should carefully seek out a fellow-practitioner bodhisattva who has already made the great vow, possesses wisdom and capability, and is able to transmit and explain the meaning of the verbal expressions [of the precepts].

Having first prostrated at the feet of such a preeminent Bodhisattva endowed with these virtues, he should bare his right shoulder, rest his knees upon the ground, join his palms in reverence, and make this request:
"Virtuous One, please take heed!"
I, who am named [Name], beg for the reception of all the pure bodhisattva precepts from the Venerable One.
I only pray that you will, out of compassion, grant them to me for a moment without declining due to weariness or fatigue.

A second and third time, he spoke in this same manner. Having thus made this unerring request, he bared his right shoulder and respectfully prostrated, making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time; to the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), attained great wisdom, and attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and before them, he focused his mindfulness on their various merits, giving rise to a profound and pure mind.

When bodhisattvas wish to confer the bodhisattva precepts upon others, they should first explain the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mātṛkā, the bodhisattva training rules, and the characteristics of transgressions, causing them to hear and receive these teachings.

Having observed one's own inclinations with wisdom, and being capable of discerning that one is able to receive the bodhisattva precepts—not merely at the urging of others nor for the sake of surpassing others—one should be known as a firm bodhisattva, fit to receive the pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) of a bodhisattva; thus, the method for receiving the precepts should be correctly bestowed accordingly.

The bodhisattva receiving the precepts, furthermore, before a wise and powerful superior bodhisattva, humbly and respectfully places his knees upon the ground; facing the Buddha image, he joins his palms and makes this request:
"I pray only that the Virtuous One will compassionately grant me the pure bodhisattva precepts."
Having made this request, he focused his mind on a single object to cultivate a pure heart, thinking:
"Before long, I shall attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed treasury of great merit."
He then remained silent, reflecting upon the meaning of these matters.
At that time, a wise and powerful bodhisattva, with an undistracted mind, whether sitting or standing, addressed that bodhisattva who was practicing right conduct, saying:
"O son of good family, [you who have such-and-such a name]!..."
"I grant you permission. Are you a bodhisattva? He should answer:
“Yes. “Have you yet made the vow for bodhicitta? One should answer:
“[It has] already been generated.
From this point forward, one should speak as follows:
“O son of good family, [you who are] named so-and-so!”
Listen, you all.

Now you wish to receive from me all the training precepts of a bodhisattva and all the pure vows of a bodhisattva—namely, the vow of restraint, the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the vow of benefiting sentient beings.

Such training rules and such pure precepts have been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past, shall be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are now being fully possessed by all bodhisattvas currently throughout the ten directions.

Regarding these points of training and these pure precepts, all bodhisattvas of the past have trained, all bodhisattvas of the future shall train, and all bodhisattvas of the present are now training.
"Are you able to accept this?
He replied, "I am able to accept it."
The Bodhisattva who bestows [the precepts] speaks thus a second and a third time; the Bodhisattva who receives [the precepts] likewise answers thus a second and a third time.

Having thus received them, the Bodhisattva who receives does not rise from his seat, while the Bodhisattva who bestows, before the image of the Buddha, pays homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently dwelling throughout the ten directions, makes offerings, and prostrates at their feet, making this declaration:
"I reverently address the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in all the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions."

"Now, herein there is a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name who, in the presence of me, [the bodhisattva] of such-and-such a name, has received the bodhisattva precepts after reciting them three times.
I bear witness to this."

I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the foremost true sages throughout the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions—who have attained manifest awakening regarding all sentient beings at all times and in all places, whether appearing or unappearing, shall likewise bear witness for this bodhisattva named [Name], who receives the precepts.
The second and third [recitations] were likewise spoken.
Thus the ritual for receiving the precepts (śīla-karman) was completed.

Immediately thereafter, before all the Buddhas currently residing in the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions, and before the bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (mahābhūmi), a natural sign appeared, indicating that this bodhisattva had received the pure precepts (viśuddha-śīla) to be undertaken by a bodhisattva.

At that time, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, beholding this natural mark of the Bodhisattva, give rise to mindfulness; through the power of mindfulness, their correct wisdom and vision are activated; and by means of correct wisdom and vision, they realize as it truly is that in such-and-such a world, a Bodhisattva of such-and-such a name has correctly received the pure precepts to be received by a Bodhisattva from such-and-such a Bodhisattva.
All those who have received the precepts here regard this bodhisattva as a son or a younger brother, giving rise to feelings of kinship, kindness, affection, and compassion.
Through the affectionate concern and compassion of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, this bodhisattva is made to seek wholesome dharmas, causing them to increase further and further without any decline.
This is called the formal announcement and request for witness when receiving the bodhisattva precepts.
"If bodhisattvas abide in the code of ethical discipline, there are four types of acts that constitute defeats."
What are these four?
If a bodhisattva, out of a desire for gain and honor, praises themselves and disparages others, this is called the first defeat (pārājika) dharma.

If a bodhisattva, while possessing material wealth, fails to give with compassion and practice generosity when those who are suffering, impoverished, and without refuge or protection come before them seeking wealth—due to a nature of stinginess regarding wealth—and likewise, when those who seek the Dharma come before them, fails to bestow it despite possessing the Dharma—due to a nature of stinginess regarding the Dharma—this is called the second *pārājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva nurtures such a form of the obsession with anger, and because of this cause and condition, does not merely initiate harsh speech and then stop, but—being obscured by anger—goes so far as to strike, injure, harm, or afflict sentient beings with hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, or staves, harboring within a fierce and intense intent of resentment;
and when another comes to admonish or apologize for an offense committed, he does not accept it, does not endure it, and does not relinquish his grudge—this is called the third *parājika* dharma.

If a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and out of a fondness for it, proclaims, reveals, and establishes counterfeit Dharma; and regarding this counterfeit Dharma, either gains personal conviction or follows others [in their acceptance], this is called the fourth defeat (pārājika) offense.
These are called the four types of defeats for a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva commits even one of these four defeats, let alone all of them, they will no longer be able to increase or gather the vast provisions for enlightenment in this present life, nor will they be able to purify their intention in this present life; such a person is called a counterfeit bodhisattva, not a true bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva violates any of the four pārājika dharmas through weak or medium-grade fetters, they do not forfeit the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline;
however, violating them through superior-grade fetters is termed forfeiture.

If a bodhisattva repeatedly commits any of the four defeats (*pārājika*), doing so entirely without shame or remorse, and even developing a deep fondness for them while perceiving them as meritorious, it should be known that this is called an offense of the highest degree of entanglement (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*); such a person is no longer a bodhisattva.
If one momentarily manifests an act constituting a defeat (*pārājika*), one immediately abandons the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
This is just as when bhikṣus commit an act of defeat, they immediately relinquish the prātimokṣa precepts.
If a bodhisattva, through such a transgression, should relinquish the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), they are capable of receiving it again within this very life;
they are not incapable, unlike a bhikṣu who, having committed a defeat (*pārājika*) while abiding in the prātimokṣa vows, is incapable of receiving them again in this very life.

"The pure ethical discipline thus undertaken by a bodhisattva is the most excellent, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and boundless among all other forms of pure ethical discipline, and is followed by a great treasury of merit."
Aroused by the most supreme and virtuous intention, it is universally capable of eliminating every kind of evil conduct of all sentient beings.

Compared to this bodhisattva’s discipline of the vows of restraint (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*), all other forms of restraint do not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part; they do not equal any numerical fraction, calculated fraction, arithmetical fraction, illustrative fraction, or even an *upaniṣad* fraction, because this [bodhisattva vow] encompasses all great merits.

Having thus performed the ritual procedures for receiving the bodhisattva precepts and so forth, both the bestower and the recipient of the precepts together arose to make offerings; they prostrated at the feet of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, and withdrew with reverence.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not seek to receive the pure bodhisattva precepts from every wise person.

One should not receive them from those who lack pure faith—meaning those who have no initial conviction or understanding regarding these pure precepts and thus cannot enter into them, or who do not engage in proper reflection. Nor should one receive them from those who possess stinginess and greed, those who are obscured by stinginess and greed, those with great desires, or those who lack contentment.

One should not receive [the precepts] from one who has violated the pure precepts, who lacks reverence for the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*), or who is negligent and lax regarding the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*).
One should not receive them from one who harbors anger and resentment, who is largely intolerant, or who is unable to endure the transgressions of others.

If there are those who are indolent or lazy, who for the most part are addicted to sleeping day and night, who delight in reclining, who delight in lying down, who delight in associating with companions, and who delight in idle chatter—one should not receive [the teachings] from them.
One whose mind is distracted—even to the extent that they cannot maintain a single-pointed cultivation of a virtuous mind for as long as it takes to milk a cow—should not be followed for instruction.
One who is obscure, of a deluded nature, of extremely inferior mind, or who slanders the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka and the Mātṛkā, should not be followed for instruction.

Furthermore, although bodhisattvas have already fully received and maintained the ultimate dharma for the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), they never hastily reveal or instruct it to sentient beings who lack faith and disparage the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Why is this? Because having heard it, they are unable to believe or understand; being shrouded by the great obscuration of ignorance, they give rise to slander.

Due to this slander, just as one who abides in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline achieves an immeasurable treasury of merit, so too does that slanderer become pursued by an immeasurable treasury of sinful karma. Until all evil speech, evil views, and evil thoughts have been permanently abandoned, he shall never escape them.

If bodhisattvas wish to receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), and if they do not encounter a person (*pudgala*) endowed with complete merit, they should at that time personally receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
One should receive it in this manner:
baring the right shoulder, placing the right knee on the ground, and speaking these words:
"I, who am named [so-and-so]..."

I prostrate and address all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages: I now wish, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, to vow to receive all the bodhisattva training rules and to vow to receive all the bodhisattva pure precepts—namely, the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

Such training rules and such pure precepts were already possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past, will be possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are now possessed by all bodhisattvas currently throughout the ten directions.

Regarding these points of training and this pure morality, all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained, all bodhisattvas of the future shall train, and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are now training.
The second and third [times] should also be spoken in this manner; having spoken, one should rise.
All that remains should be understood as before. 2.

The Ritual for Confessing Faults (*Āpatti-pratideśanā-karman*). Second: If a bodhisattva, having correctly received the code of discipline (*saṃvara*) from another, gives rise to the most extreme respect and reverence through a well-purified intention to train, an intention for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and an intention to benefit all sentient beings.

From the very beginning, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and not commit any transgression; should a transgression occur, one must immediately repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma so that purity may be restored.

One should know that all such transgressions by a bodhisattva are subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and should be confessed and extinguished before a person of authority who understands the meaning of verbal expression and is capable of awakening to and accepting both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna.

If a bodhisattva violates any of the aforementioned rules of defeat (*pārājika*) through a superior degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), they lose the vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) and must receive it again.

If they violate any of the aforementioned rules of defeat through a middling degree of entanglement, they should confess and purify the fault before three persons or more, in accordance with the ritual for the disclosure and removal of evil deeds.
First, one should state the name of the offense committed, speaking as follows:
"Venerable One, [or: Great Virtue], I, who am named so-and-so, have transgressed the Bodhisattva Vinaya rules."
Regarding the matter as it was described, one incurs an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta*;
the rest is to be explained in the same manner as the method for confessing and extinguishing an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta* according to the rules for *bhikṣus*.

If one commits an offense against the aforementioned rules of defeat (*pārājika*) or other offenses due to minor entanglements (*mṛdu-paryavasthāna*), the method for confessing before a single person (*pudgala*) should be understood as being the same as previously stated.
If there is no person to whom one may confess and purify the transgression,
the bodhisattva then generates a vow of self-commitment with a pure intention:
"I shall certainly guard myself against the future and never commit it again."
"In this way, one emerges from and becomes purified of transgressions. 3.
The Distinctions of Acquiring and Abandoning (The Third Section). Briefly stated, the bodhisattva's vow of pure ethical discipline is abandoned due to two conditions:

first, the abandonment of the great aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; second, the commission of a defeat (pārājika) through the manifestation of a superior degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*).

If bodhisattvas, even as they transform their bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions, do not abandon the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) in whatever place they are born;

because of this, these bodhisattvas do not abandon the great vow for unsurpassed enlightenment, nor do they manifest the commission of a defeat (*pārājika*) through the operation of superior-level fetters (*saṃyojana*).

If bodhisattvas undergo subsequent births and forget their original resolve, yet encounter virtuous friends who wish to awaken their mindfulness of the bodhisattva precepts, they may receive them again and again; however, this is not a new reception, nor is it a new attainment.
Preface to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman*, composed by the Śramaṇa Jingmai. The vast expanse of the ocean gathers all flowing rivers as they turn toward the source;
the profound mystery of the Dharma-nature unifies all phenomena within its universal assembly.

Thus we know that the non-explanation reveals the Way, honoring the silence of Vaiśālī; by cutting off hearing, it honors the closing of the room at Magadha where flowers rained down. Were it not for a foundation of virtue so vast and profound, who could fathom its grand significance?
There was a Dharma Master of the Tripiṭaka, known as Xuánzàng.
In his tender youth, he transcended the mundane world, concentrating his spirit and vital energy amidst the white clouds;
in his prime, his ambition roamed the realm of truth, clarifying the radiance of wisdom within the profound and mysterious.
Those who rinse their mouths at its source encounter it without realizing it; those who bathe in its current swim within it without fathoming it.
When the Great Tortoise revealed the year of his extinction, he cast aside his hairpins and finger-guards to cultivate the flower fields;
in the year that Sūdarśana sought the Way, he polished his precept-jewel to frolic across the earth.

Thus, during the final years of the flaming Sui dynasty, when the Three Collections first received imperial patronage, he reflected deeply upon the essential meaning of the teachings and realized that the existing expositions were still incomplete. Lamenting the disordered translations of the sacred texts and grieving over the erroneous transmission of the divine principles, he was able to depart from the Jade Gate and travel afar, reaching the Golden River to devote himself to the sublime Dharma.
There was a great treasury of the True Dharma, truly named Śīlabhadra.

His realization of the Way reached the four reliances, and his fame spread throughout the five regions of India; for all those who sought the ocean of the Tripitaka, he was the one from whom they took their standard. Thus, the precepts he upheld became the hallmark of his magnificent reputation.
Consequently, in the kingdom of Magadha, he reverently received the casket and staff, seeing what had never been seen before and hearing what had never been heard before;
even the meeting between Sātavāhana and Dharmarakṣa could not surpass this.
I earnestly entreated him to receive the Bodhisattva precepts; after three prayers over one year, my fervent hope was finally granted.
Through the pure precepts of a Bodhisattva, the Dharma Master realized the constant norms of the One Vehicle;
through the grand protocol of transmission and reception, he believed in the great statutes of the Ten Stages.
What I have specially contemplated and savored has never ceased to resonate in my throat and breast.

On the day of the first moon of the month marking the beginning of the Emperor’s reign over the world, in the twenty-third year of the Great Tang’s Zhenguan era, I received an imperial decree at Daci’en Monastery to translate the *Bhikṣu-karmavācanā-pratimokṣa-sūtra*. Thus, two fascicles were opened, which constitute the flowing current of the Bodhisattva’s stages of perfection.

I, Mai, being of dull wit, have been unworthily included among the ranks of translators. Having personally received these grand instructions and witnessed the transmission of this flame of the Dharma, my heart was moved and I expressed my sentiments through speech to extol this Great Way. I have thus briefly recorded the time of this translation so that it may serve as a reminder against forgetfulness.

As for the verification of the meaning, the verification of the text, the standardization of characters, and the transcription, approximately twenty śramaṇas of the Yijie (Vinaya) school, including Mingyan and others, each presided over their respective tasks, collectively supporting the purport of the teaching.
The Ritual Text for the Bodhisattva Precepts (Bodhisattva-śīla-karman)
